title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
summary: How hardware enforces two privilege levels, why user code can't touch hardware directly, and what actually happens on a mode switch.

slides.markdown:
Every modern CPU has at least two privilege levels: **user mode**, where ordinary programs run with restricted powers, and **kernel mode**, where the OS runs with full hardware access. This split exists so a buggy or malicious program can never crash the whole machine or read another process's memory directly.

Think of it like a hotel: guests (user-mode programs) have a keycard that opens their own room and common areas, but only staff (the kernel) hold the master key to every room, the boiler room, and the wiring. Everything in this topic is really one question: how does hardware make that guarantee unbreakable in software?

slides.sectionTitle: The mode bit: how hardware enforces two privilege levels
slides.markdown:
The CPU keeps a **mode bit** (or a small privilege field) in a protected register that software cannot freely rewrite. When it's set to 0, the CPU is in kernel mode and every instruction is legal; set to 1, it's in user mode and the CPU hardware itself refuses to execute privileged instructions or access certain memory and I/O ports.

This is enforced in silicon, not convention — a user-mode program that tries to execute a privileged instruction doesn't get ignored, it triggers a **general protection fault**, and the kernel decides what happens next (usually killing the offending process).

The key idea: privilege separation isn't a polite agreement between programs, it's a hardware trap door that closes automatically the instant something oversteps.

slides.sectionTitle: What kernel mode can do that user mode can't
slides.markdown:
Kernel mode can execute **privileged instructions** — halting the CPU, changing the memory-mapping tables, disabling interrupts, directly programming a disk controller's registers. User mode is blocked from all of these by hardware.

User mode can still touch memory and do I/O, just indirectly and under supervision: it reads and writes only the virtual addresses the kernel has mapped for it, and it performs I/O by asking the kernel to do it on its behalf via a system call, never by writing to a device's registers itself.

The practical effect: a user program cannot read another process's memory, cannot deny another process the CPU by disabling interrupts, and cannot brick the disk controller with a bad command — all three require kernel-only instructions.

![x86 privilege ring hierarchy](assets/privilege-rings.svg)

x86 hardware actually defines **four** rings, not two, but general-purpose OSes like Linux and Windows only use two of them in practice: **Ring 0** for the kernel and **Ring 3** for everything else. Rings 1 and 2 exist in the spec for finer-grained privilege (some older OSes and certain driver models used them) but mainstream OSes skip them — the two-level split is simpler to reason about and enforce.

Modern virtualization adds a wrinkle: hypervisors introduced a "ring -1" concept (VMX root mode on Intel) so a hypervisor can sit even below Ring 0 and control guest kernels that still believe they're running in Ring 0.

slides.sectionTitle: How a user process asks the kernel for help: the trap mechanism
slides.markdown:
A user process can't just "call into" kernel code the way it calls its own functions — jumping to an arbitrary kernel address would defeat the whole point of privilege separation. Instead it executes a special **trap instruction** (`syscall` on x86-64, `svc` on ARM) that the hardware treats as a controlled, single entry point into the kernel.

The trap does three things atomically: switches the mode bit to kernel mode, jumps to a fixed, kernel-chosen handler address (never an address the user process supplies), and saves enough user-mode state (registers, program counter) to resume afterward.

This is why a rogue program can't forge its way into arbitrary kernel code — the entry point is fixed by the kernel at boot, not chosen by the caller.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: user mode / kernel mode transition on a syscall
slides.markdown:
![Mode switch timeline on a syscall](assets/mode-switch-timeline.svg)

Each crossing between lanes is a full mode switch: the CPU flips its privilege level, and the kernel saves/restores registers so the user process resumes exactly where it left off, unaware (functionally) that a whole kernel handler ran in between.

This round trip is not free — see the pitfall slide for why treating it as free is a common mistake.

slides.sectionTitle: Why not just run everything in kernel mode?
slides.markdown:
It would remove all mode-switch overhead — no trap, no register save/restore, no CPU privilege flip. Some real systems do exactly this: unikernels and certain embedded RTOSes run the entire application in one privilege level for speed and simplicity, accepting the risk because the workload is tightly controlled and trusted.

For a general-purpose OS running arbitrary, often untrusted applications, the trade-off flips: without the hardware wall, one buggy pointer dereference in a web browser could overwrite kernel memory and crash or compromise the entire machine, not just that one tab.

The rule of thumb: privilege separation is a tax you pay for fault isolation, and you can only skip it when you fully trust every piece of code sharing the machine.

slides.sectionTitle: Kernel panics vs user process crashes
slides.markdown:
The privilege split explains why the same category of bug has wildly different blast radii depending on which mode it happens in.

| | User process crash | Kernel panic |
|---|---|---|
| Scope of failure | That one process only | Entire machine |
| OS response | Kill the process, reclaim its memory, continue running everything else | Halt or reboot — the kernel can no longer trust its own state |
| Typical cause | Null pointer, divide-by-zero, out-of-bounds access in app code | Bad driver, corrupted kernel data structure, hardware fault |
| Recovery | Instant, invisible to other processes | Full reboot, or at minimum losing all running state |

**How to decide what you're looking at:** if other applications keep running normally, it's a user-mode crash; if the whole system freezes or reboots, the fault happened in kernel mode where isolation no longer applies.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: treating a mode switch as free
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A system call is basically just a function call — negligible overhead."

**Why it's wrong:** a mode switch costs real cycles beyond the work it performs — saving and restoring registers, flushing or invalidating parts of the CPU pipeline and TLB, and (on modern CPUs) paying Meltdown/Spectre-mitigation costs that specifically target the user/kernel boundary. On typical hardware a syscall round trip runs several hundred nanoseconds to a few microseconds, roughly 10–100x a plain function call — trivial once, expensive in a tight loop doing millions of them.

**Correct model:** batch or avoid syscalls in hot paths — this is exactly why `read()`/`write()` are buffered in userspace, why `io_uring` exists to amortize the mode-switch cost over many I/O operations, and why a database doing one `write()` per row instead of buffering is a classic performance bug.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: how debuggers and antivirus tools bend this boundary
slides.markdown:
Some tools appear to break the user/kernel wall, but they don't — they use kernel-provided, controlled hooks. A debugger like `gdb` uses the `ptrace` syscall, which the kernel exposes specifically so one (permitted) user process can inspect and control another's registers and memory — still mediated entirely by the kernel, not a direct memory poke.

Antivirus and EDR (endpoint detection and response) software historically ran kernel-mode drivers for deep visibility — process creation, file writes, network activity — because user-mode-only tools can't see or intercept everything happening in the kernel. This is a real trade-off: kernel-mode drivers see more but a bug in one can crash the whole machine, which is exactly the failure mode behind several major real-world outages involving faulty AV/EDR kernel drivers.

The nuance for an interview: "can user-mode code observe kernel behavior" — yes, but only through interfaces the kernel deliberately exposes, never by reaching across the boundary uninvited.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
Profiling tools report **user time** vs **system (kernel) time** precisely because of this boundary — `top` and `time` split CPU usage into `%usr` and `%sys` columns. A process pegged at high `%sys` is spending its time in the kernel (heavy syscalls, page faults, context switches), which points you toward I/O patterns or lock contention, not application logic — a very different fix than high `%usr`, which points at your own code.

Container runtimes also live at this boundary: a container's processes run in user mode against the *same* host kernel as everything else on the machine, sharing one kernel-mode implementation — which is exactly why a kernel security bug can be exploited to escape container isolation, unlike a VM where each guest has its own kernel.

When you next see a `%sys` spike in a dashboard, this topic is the reason it means something specific: kernel-mode work, not your business logic, is where the time is going.
